naturalness.evidence: “What religious objects did the spies say were in one of the houses?” is an idiomatic reported-speech question.

processing.evidence: Readers must carry “What religious objects” into “the spies say were,” but this single reporting layer is manageable and expresses the requested report directly.

context_economy.evidence: “The spies” and “in one of the houses” identify the report being asked about without adding unrelated setup.

structure_assessments.reason: “Did the spies say were” introduces only one reporting layer. Identifying the objects within that report requires no avoidable reconstruction.

naturalness.evidence: “What did Athaliah see before she tore her clothes?” is direct, idiomatic English.

processing.evidence: In “Athaliah see before she tore her clothes,” both “she” and “her” refer clearly to Athaliah, and the event sequence is readily parsed.

context_economy.evidence: “Before she tore her clothes” supplies the temporal relationship being tested rather than extraneous background.

structure_assessments.reason: The local references in “she tore her clothes” have a single clear antecedent, and the before-clause states the relevant temporal relationship.

naturalness.evidence: “When did Jotham address Shechem's leaders?” is a conventional, naturally phrased question.

processing.evidence: “Jotham” is explicitly the speaker and “Shechem's leaders” the audience; the short question requires no syntactic reconstruction.

context_economy.evidence: The question contains only the event whose timing is requested: “Jotham address Shechem's leaders.”

naturalness.evidence: “Handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched Paul were taken to the sick” is grammatical and idiomatic despite its length.

processing.evidence: Readers retain “handkerchiefs and aprons” through “that had touched Paul” before reaching “were taken.” This is a manageable demand, and the modifier and transfer event express the relevant circumstances.

context_economy.evidence: The contact with Paul and transport “to the sick” identify the event whose outcome is requested; they are useful context rather than excess setup.

structure_assessments.reason: The relative clause “that had touched Paul” naturally describes the coordinated cloth items. Its placement creates only a short, ordinary interruption before “were taken.”
The cloths remain the subject through contact and transport, while “to the sick” clearly identifies the recipients. The passive does not require readers to infer a carrier.

naturalness.evidence: “Why does Uzziah live in a separate house until he dies?” uses an acceptable narrative present. Options such as “He was a priest” and “He was a leper” are straightforward status statements.

processing.evidence: “He” in “until he dies” clearly refers to Uzziah. The parallel “He was a…” options are easy to compare.

context_economy.evidence: “In a separate house until he dies” identifies the living arrangement and its duration without unrelated framing.

structure_assessments.reason: “Until he dies” has a clear subject and marks the endpoint of the residence. Neither the reference nor the temporal clause adds avoidable decoding.

naturalness.evidence: “What does Zebul tell Gaal to do?” is idiomatic, and the action options, including “Flee the city” and “Fight Abimelech,” are naturally phrased.

processing.evidence: The “tell Gaal to do” construction clearly makes Gaal the intended actor. The substantive options are short, parallel action phrases.

context_economy.evidence: The question names only the instructor, “Zebul,” and recipient, “Gaal,” needed to identify the instruction.

structure_assessments.reason: “Zebul tell Gaal to do” explicitly distinguishes the instructor from the performer through a familiar English construction.

naturalness.evidence: “What pact did 40 Jewish men make?” is grammatical and idiomatic; “make” naturally combines with “pact.”

processing.evidence: “40 Jewish men” is a simple subject phrase, and “What pact” directly requests the agreement's content.

context_economy.evidence: “40 Jewish men” briefly identifies the group; there is no extended or distracting setup.

naturalness.evidence: “What did five men from Dan want in Laish?” is understandable, but “want in Laish” is slightly loose phrasing for an aim concerning that place.

processing.evidence: Readers must interpret “in Laish” as locating the desired objective rather than simply the men or their wanting. This is a minor attachment demand, not substantial decoding.

context_economy.evidence: “Five men from Dan” and “in Laish” identify the participants and location without excess background.

naturalness.evidence: “Non-serving groups” is an unnatural, underspecified label for divisions going off duty. Readers must mentally repair what kind of service “non-serving” excludes.

processing.evidence: “Non-serving groups” requires readers to infer an unstated duty category and reconcile being “non-serving” with performing an assignment such as “Guard the house of Yahweh.” This avoidable status-decoding step goes beyond identifying the assignment.

context_economy.evidence: “On the Sabbath” and the group designation serve to identify the relevant assignment. The problem is the wording of “non-serving,” not excess context.

structure_assessments.reason: “Non-serving groups” leaves the service domain unstated and can initially suggest groups performing no service at all. Recovering the intended off-duty status adds unnecessary interpretation.

naturalness.evidence: “What does the old prophet tell the man of God?” is a natural question. “The man of God” functions as a coherent descriptive title.

processing.evidence: “The old prophet” is clearly the speaker and “the man of God” the recipient. The question itself introduces no nested quotation or difficult reference chain.

context_economy.evidence: The two descriptions in “the old prophet tell the man of God” economically distinguish the participants.

structure_assessments.reason: The word order in “the old prophet tell the man of God” explicitly assigns speaker and recipient roles without requiring inference about who addresses whom.

naturalness.evidence: “When would Felix hear Paul's case?” uses the familiar, idiomatic expression “hear a case.”

processing.evidence: “Felix” is the named hearer, and “Paul's case” directly identifies the legal matter. The when-question is readily parsed.

context_economy.evidence: “When would Felix hear Paul's case?” contains no setup beyond the event whose timing is requested.

naturalness.evidence: “What does Uzziah do to Eloth as king?” is slightly stiff in its broad “do to” phrasing. The present-tense stem also shifts to past-tense options such as “Sold it” and “Rebuilt and restored it.”

processing.evidence: “As king” is readily understood as describing Uzziah, and “it” in the short options clearly refers to Eloth. Comparing the actions requires no substantial reconstruction.

context_economy.evidence: “As king” is a brief role cue, not an extended or distracting introduction.

structure_assessments.reason: In “Rebuilt and restored it,” the adjacent coordinated verbs naturally share “it,” whose antecedent is the explicitly named Eloth.
